comment: Sender pre-flight conformance fixture (SPEC.md 6.4b). Pins the local-refusal decisions a sending SDK MUST make before publishing: sender text against the recipient's declared cap or the 22.5 default, the serialized envelope against the transport's advertised maximum payload (18.9), and content types against the manifest (8.1) - each refused locally with the SAME error code the recipient would answer with, so a pre-flight refusal and a remote refusal are indistinguishable to the caller's error handling. One file per concern: this is the sibling of accept-signal.json. THE FIXTURE IS THE AUTHORITY: when a test against it fails, fix the implementation, and when the fixture itself is believed wrong, change it only with a spec change alongside.
spec: SPEC.md 6.4b (sender pre-flight), 22.5 (cap, extraction ladder, UTF-16 measurement), 18.9 (max payload), 8.1/8.2 (limits, rate_limits, skills), 12.2 (codes)

identities.comment: The same published test vectors budget.json and inbound-protections.json use, deliberately: they are not real identities and control nothing, and reusing them keeps any new private-key-shaped string out of the repository. Nothing in this fixture is signed - every case pins a LOCAL decision made before an envelope is published, so there are no wire bytes to sign.

measurement.comment: The sender measures exactly as the receiver would (6.4b), or the mirror is broken by construction.
measurement.unit: UTF-16 code units of the extracted sender text - not bytes, not scalar values; U+1F600 counts 2 (22.5)
measurement.extraction: the 22.5 ladder, unchanged: a string payload is the text; else walk text, message, prompt; else compact JSON of the payload is what gets measured
measurement.comparison: strictly greater-than: a message AT the cap is legal and MUST be published (22.5)

sender_text.comment: declared_cap null means the recipient's manifest declares no limits.max_inbound_chars (8.1), so the 22.5 default governs. The three shapes the spec names: at-cap, the over-cap boundary, and the undeclared default.

cases.why: at the cap is legal - the comparison is strictly greater-than
the boundary case: one unit over the declared cap refuses locally with the code 22.5 would answer with
no declared cap: the 22.5 default (65,536) governs, and at the default is legal
no declared cap: one unit over the 22.5 default refuses locally
U+1F600 counts 2 code units, plus 'a' is 3 - at the cap. The unit must match 22.5's exactly or one side refuses what the other accepts
two astral characters are 4 code units, over a cap of 3 - an implementation counting scalar values (2) would wrongly publish

envelope_size.comment: Against the transport's advertised maximum payload (18.9). This is the one pre-flight check with no remote mirror: an oversized publish never reaches the recipient at all - the transport refuses it - so the pre-flight turns a raw transport error into a deterministic, protocol-legible local refusal under the same code a caller already handles for 'too large'. error.details names the limit that fired so an operator can tell the two refusals apart; the CODE is the same so a caller's error handling never has to.

cases.why: at the transport bound is legal - the transport accepts payloads up to and including its maximum
one byte over is refused before publish; 18.9's remedy (an Object Store ref part) is the correct path for the content

content_type.comment: Against the recipient's manifest (8.1): the skill's output_modes must be able to satisfy the request's config.accepted_output, and the input's type must be within the skill's input_modes. Refusal code is the one 6.4 answers with.

cases.why: at least one requested output mode is one the skill produces
no requested output mode is one the skill produces - the recipient would refuse with this exact code, so the sender does, locally

mirror.comment: The point of the whole file: a pre-flight refusal and a remote refusal carry the same error code and the same retryable, so they are indistinguishable to the caller's error handling. What differs is scope, not shape: a pre-flight refusal is local - nothing was published, so nothing was signed, deduplicated, or retried - and its error.details MAY name the limit that fired.

not_covered.comment: Boundaries, written down so nobody mistakes them for gaps.
items: rate_limits throttling is a SHOULD (6.4b) and timing-dependent; it pins no byte and is not cased here.
Whether the recipient's DECLARED cap is true is the recipient's problem: a wrong declaration yields a remote refusal, and the mirror already makes that indistinguishable to the caller.

A recipient running a nonstandard cap it never declared (22.5): senders pre-flight against the default, and the divergence resolves remotely - which is the round trip 8.1's limits block exists to spare.
